segments.say: In the fourth century, in the deserts of Egypt, there were communities of Christian monks who had withdrawn from the world to live lives of prayer and simplicity. One of them, a monk named Evagrius Ponticus, wrote detailed descriptions of the struggles that monks faced. And one of these struggles he called acedia.

Evagrius described acedia as one of the most troublesome of all the temptations. He called it the noonday demon, because it often struck in the middle of the day, around noon, when the sun was high and the hours seemed endless. The monk would feel restless, unable to focus on prayer or work, constantly looking out of the window, watching the sun to see how long it was until the meal.

Reading Evagrius's descriptions today, many people find them strikingly familiar. The restlessness. The checking of the time. The feeling that the day will never end. The urge to go somewhere else, to visit someone, to do anything other than what one is supposed to be doing. It sounds a lot like boredom, mixed with a kind of spiritual weariness.

Scholars point out that acedia was more than simple boredom. It included a sense of listlessness, a loss of care, a temptation to abandon one's commitments. In later Christian traditions, it was sometimes linked to sloth, one of the seven deadly sins. But at its heart, it described a familiar human experience. The struggle to stay engaged with a meaningful but monotonous life.

What did the monks recommend? Evagrius and others suggested several remedies. Staying in place, rather than fleeing. Continuing with small tasks, like weaving baskets, even when motivation was low. Remembering the deeper purpose of their life. And patience, trusting that the feeling would pass. Some of these sound remarkably like modern advice.

The idea of staying with the feeling, rather than running from it, echoes what we've learned from John Cage and from mindfulness. And the idea of continuing with small, simple tasks echoes the research on tiny habits and momentum. Ancient monks and modern psychologists, separated by sixteen centuries, arriving at similar insights.

The monks also emphasized remembering the purpose behind their daily routines. Their prayers and tasks were connected to something they deeply valued. This connects to modern research on boredom and meaning. When we remember why we do what we do, the monotony becomes easier to bear.

It's also fascinating that Evagrius noticed the timing. The noonday demon struck in the middle of the day. Today, we might connect that to the afternoon dip in alertness, built into our body clocks. The monks may have been observing a natural rhythm, and interpreting it in their own spiritual language.

I find it comforting to know that people sixteen hundred years ago, living very different lives, struggled with something so similar to what we feel in a dull meeting or on a slow afternoon. Boredom, restlessness, the longing for something else. It's one of the threads that connects human beings across the centuries.

And the monks' simplest remedy might be the gentlest of all. Patience. The feeling will pass. The afternoon will end. The evening will come, and then the night, with its rest. Tonight, you've reached that rest. The noonday demon has long gone home.

So here's what the noonday demon teaches us. Desert monks in the fourth century described acedia, a restless, weary state that often struck around noon. Their remedies included staying put, continuing small tasks, remembering their purpose, and patience. And their insights echo much of what modern psychology says about boredom today.

show.title: The noonday demon
items: It struck around noon, with restless clock watching
Remedies: stay, keep to small tasks, remember purpose
Ancient and modern advice often agree

segments.say: So what's happening in the brain when we're bored? Neuroscientists have started to look at this question, and their findings connect boredom to attention, to the wandering mind, and to the search for reward.
